abstract: OpenAI Economic Research report by Chris Liao, Carl Shan and Aaron Chatterji, dated November 6, 2026, studying how academic scientists use AI. It analyses 580,186 scientific messages sent over a 34-day span in 2026 by 1,819 scientists enrolled in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers plan, mapped to a 40-task, 10-workflow taxonomy by privacy-preserving classifiers, and pairs that with a survey of the same population fielded September 30 to October 7, 2026. Four findings: use concentrates in a few activities, with reading and writing alone over half of the average scientist's scientific messages; AI shapes which ideas scientists pursue and how they refine them; scientists stay involved in execution, following up after about a third of requests and more often where more expertise is required; and 98 percent of survey respondents expect AI to increase the rate of discovery in their field.
keyFindings: 85 percent of the average scientist's scientific messages to ChatGPT and Codex fall in four workflows - reading and knowledge acquisition, scientific analysis, software development, and writing - and reading and writing alone account for over half.

Self-reported productivity ratios, defined as the time a task would need without AI divided by the time it needs with AI at the same quality, range from a mean of 1.35x in administrative work to 2.83x in research software and code development. Reported AI time share and reported productivity gain correlate at 0.96 across the eight workflow averages.
98 percent of survey respondents expect AI to increase the rate of scientific discovery in their field, most often citing faster completion of research tasks.

The most common obstacle is verification: 45.4 percent of scientists selected 'time needed to check or correct outputs' as a difficulty in obtaining value from ChatGPT, the single most-chosen response.

Scientists follow up on AI output after about one-third of requests on average, and follow up more often within the same task when the request requires greater scientific expertise - evidence that use is assistive rather than end-to-end.

AI use is thinnest in precisely the workflows the authors flag as bottlenecks: scientists report using AI for 17.6 percent of their time in data gathering, 11.8 percent in peer review and service, and 11.4 percent in administration. The authors argue gains elsewhere may not translate into overall scientific progress while these remain.

On ideation the division of labour differs by stage: when exploring research directions scientists often ask AI to propose what to investigate, while when developing specific research questions they typically supply the question and ask AI to refine or evaluate it.
methodology: Usage data covers 1,819 scientists on the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers plan who sent 580,186 messages about scientific work over a 34-day span in 2026. Messages were mapped to one of 10 scientific workflows and, within each, a specific task, using a taxonomy based on SciNet, with additional classifications for ideation role and execution follow-up. All classification ran through privacy-preserving classifiers and the authors state that at no point did researchers observe the underlying messages. Comparisons span seven fields (biology, chemistry and materials, computer science, earth and planetary sciences, engineering, mathematics, physics) and three age groups (18-29, 30-39, 40 and older), with age comparisons covering 1,640 scientists after excluding 179 with missing data. The survey was fielded 2026-09-30 to 2026-10-07 with 249-251 scientists contributing paired values per workflow; AI time share and productivity ratio were both collected as banded response options converted to midpoints.
qualifiers: The sample is scientists who chose to enrol in a paid academic ChatGPT plan, so it is self-selected among AI users and carries no population denominator; nothing here estimates the share of scientists or of workers using AI, which is why it sits on genai-work-adoption as a directional signal rather than a data point. The productivity ratios are self-reported against a counterfactual the respondent imagines, collected in wide bands and converted to midpoints, with 'less time' coded as 0.5 and '400 percent or more' as 5; they are not measured time savings and should not be mixed with the controlled studies behind the site's productivity figure. The 0.96 correlation between use and reported gain is cross-workflow and consistent with scientists choosing to use AI where they already expect it to help, which the authors say explicitly - it is not evidence of a causal effect. Usage covers a single 34-day window. OpenAI is both the platform operator and the author, and one author is a paid OpenAI contractor; Tier 2 accordingly.
